claim: Nova1/2 double knockout (dKO) dampens DCC signaling by reducing the full-length Dcclong isoform while increasing the truncated Dccshort isoform.
source: We reported previously that Nova1/2 double knockout (dKO) dampens DCC signaling by reducing the full-length Dcclong isoform while increasing the truncated Dccshort isoform, which results in delayed commissural neuron migration and axonal projection toward the midline (Leggere et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication (Leggere et al., 2016).

claim: Nova1/2 dKO results in delayed commissural neuron migration and axonal projection toward the midline.
source: We reported previously that Nova1/2 double knockout (dKO) dampens DCC signaling by reducing the full-length Dcclong isoform while increasing the truncated Dccshort isoform, which results in delayed commissural neuron migration and axonal projection toward the midline (Leggere et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication (Leggere et al., 2016).

claim: The defect in Nova1/2 dKO is partial and is somewhat alleviated over time from E10.5 to E12.5.
source: As the defect is partial and is somewhat alleviated over time (from E10.5 to E12.5), some Nova1/2 dKO axons are able to reach the midline at later stages (Leggere et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication (Leggere et al., 2016).

claim: Some Nova1/2 dKO axons are able to reach the midline at later stages.
source: As the defect is partial and is somewhat alleviated over time (from E10.5 to E12.5), some Nova1/2 dKO axons are able to reach the midline at later stages (Leggere et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication (Leggere et al., 2016).

claim: At E12.5, approximately half of the axons that had reached the midline failed to cross and turned longitudinally on the ipsilateral side in Nova1/2 dKO embryos.
source: At E12.5, we found that approximately half of the axons that had reached the midline failed to cross and turned longitudinally on the ipsilateral side in Nova1/2 dKO embryos (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DiI labeling shown in Figure 1.

claim: Some postcrossing axons projected away from the midline at greater angles in Nova1/2 dKO mutants than in the wildtype controls.
source: In addition, some postcrossing axons projected away from the midline at greater angles in Nova1/2 dKO mutants than in the wildtype (WT) controls (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DiI labeling shown in Figure 1.

claim: Loss of Nova1/2 causes additional guidance abnormalities in spinal commissural axons in addition to those reported previously.
source: Thus, loss of Nova1/2 causes additional guidance abnormalities in spinal commissural axons in addition to those we reported previously.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed midline crossing and postcrossing defects.

claim: Nova1/2 dKO and Dcc single KO embryos exhibited reduced ventral commissures.
source: Using anti-ROBO3 to label axons approaching and crossing the midline, we found that Nova1/2 dKO and Dcc single KO embryos exhibited reduced ventral commissures as previously reported (Leggere et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2014), and that Dcc; Nova1; Nova2 triple KO embryos had even thinner commissures than Dcc single KO mutants (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from anti-ROBO3 staining shown in Figure 2A,B and citations to previous publications (Leggere et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2014).

claim: Dcc; Nova1; Nova2 triple KO embryos had even thinner commissures than Dcc single KO mutants.
source: Using anti-ROBO3 to label axons approaching and crossing the midline, we found that Nova1/2 dKO and Dcc single KO embryos exhibited reduced ventral commissures as previously reported (Leggere et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2014), and that Dcc; Nova1; Nova2 triple KO embryos had even thinner commissures than Dcc single KO mutants (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from anti-ROBO3 staining shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Loss of Nova1/2 is likely to affect additional guidance signaling besides reducing DCC attraction.
source: This suggests that loss of Nova1/2 is likely to affect additional guidance signaling besides reducing DCC attraction.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that triple KO mutants have more severe defects than Dcc single KO.

claim: Blocked midline crossing has been reported in Robo3 KO embryos, where all commissural axons fail to cross.
source: Blocked midline crossing has also been reported in Robo3 KO embryos, where all commissural axons fail to cross and become abnormally sensitive to the SLIT2 repellent in explants (Sabatier et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication (Sabatier et al., 2004).

claim: Robo3 KO commissural axons become abnormally sensitive to the SLIT2 repellent in explants.
source: Blocked midline crossing has also been reported in Robo3 KO embryos, where all commissural axons fail to cross and become abnormally sensitive to the SLIT2 repellent in explants (Sabatier et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication (Sabatier et al., 2004).

claim: The crossing defect in Robo3 KO mutants can be partially rescued by deleting Robo1/2 together, which allows about half of the axons to cross.
source: The crossing defect in Robo3 KO mutants can be partially rescued by deleting Robo1/2 together, which allows about half of the axons to cross (Jaworski et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication (Jaworski et al., 2010).

claim: Deleting Robo1 alone has a mild rescue effect on the Robo3 KO crossing defect.
source: Deleting Robo1 alone has a mild rescue effect and deleting Robo2 alone cannot rescue (Jaworski et al., 2010; Sabatier et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Jaworski et al., 2010; Sabatier et al., 2004).

claim: Deleting Robo2 alone cannot rescue the Robo3 KO crossing defect.
source: Deleting Robo1 alone has a mild rescue effect and deleting Robo2 alone cannot rescue (Jaworski et al., 2010; Sabatier et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Jaworski et al., 2010; Sabatier et al., 2004).

claim: In the absence of Robo3, elevated ROBO1/2 activity can block midline crossing.
source: These findings suggest that in the absence of Robo3, elevated ROBO1/2 activity can block midline crossing.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the rescue experiments in Robo3 KO mutants.

claim: Robo1 single KO embryos have a normal commissure size.
source: Robo1 single KO embryos have a normal commissure size (Jaworski et al., 2010), and by anti-ROBO3 staining, we found that Nova1; Nova2; Robo1 triple KO mutants had slightly thicker commissures than Nova1/2 dKO embryos (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication (Jaworski et al., 2010).

claim: Nova1; Nova2; Robo1 triple KO mutants had slightly thicker commissures than Nova1/2 dKO embryos.
source: Robo1 single KO embryos have a normal commissure size (Jaworski et al., 2010), and by anti-ROBO3 staining, we found that Nova1; Nova2; Robo1 triple KO mutants had slightly thicker commissures than Nova1/2 dKO embryos (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from anti-ROBO3 staining shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Most of the axons that were able to reach the midline were also able to cross in Nova1; Nova2; Robo1 triple KO embryos.
source: Using DiI labeling, we further examined midline crossing in Nova1; Nova2; Robo1 triple KO embryos and found that most of the axons that were able to reach the midline were also able to cross (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DiI labeling shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: The blocked midline crossing in Nova1/2 dKO embryos is most likely caused by elevated ROBO repulsion.
source: Thus, the blocked midline crossing in Nova1/2 dKO embryos is most likely caused by elevated ROBO repulsion.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the rescue experiments with Robo1 deletion.

claim: Nova1/2 double Het (dHet) or Robo3 single Het mutants did not exhibit any midline crossing defect.
source: Nova1/2 double Het (dHet) or Robo3 single Het mutants did not exhibit any midline crossing defect (Figure 2C,D) (Sabatier et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DiI labeling shown in Figure 2C,D and a citation to a previous publication (Sabatier et al., 2004).

claim: The triple Het mutants (Nova1/2 dHet; Robo3 Het) displayed midline crossing failure as severe as in Nova1/2 dKO embryos.
source: However, the triple Het mutants displayed midline crossing failure as severe as in Nova1/2 dKO embryos (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DiI labeling shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Nova1/2 and Robo3 have a synergistic interaction with regard to repressing midline repulsion and allowing axonal entry.
source: Therefore, Nova1/2 and Robo3 have a synergistic interaction with regard to repressing midline repulsion and allowing axonal entry.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the genetic interaction experiments.

claim: Nova1/2 are both expressed by commissural neurons and their progenitors.
source: We previously reported that Nova1/2 are both expressed by commissural neurons and their progenitors, and that Robo3 expression and alternative splicing are not altered by Nova1/2 dKO (Leggere et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication (Leggere et al., 2016).

claim: Robo3 expression and alternative splicing are not altered by Nova1/2 dKO.
source: We previously reported that Nova1/2 are both expressed by commissural neurons and their progenitors, and that Robo3 expression and alternative splicing are not altered by Nova1/2 dKO (Leggere et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication (Leggere et al., 2016).

claim: The total mRNA and protein levels of Robo1 and Robo2 were not altered by Nova1/2 dKO.
source: With respect to Robo1 and Robo2, quantitative RT-PCR and western blotting analyses showed that the total mRNA and protein levels were not altered by Nova1/2 dKO (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from quantitative RT-PCR and western blotting shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Most alternative sequences in the promoter and coding regions of Robo1 and Robo2 were not affected by Nova1/2 dKO.
source: In addition, quantitative and semi-quantitative RT-PCR showed that most alternative sequences in the promoter and coding regions were not affected; however, the inclusion of microexon 6b in both Robo1 and Robo2 was significantly increased in Nova1/2 dKO embryos (Figure 3A,B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR shown in Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The inclusion of microexon 6b in both Robo1 and Robo2 was significantly increased in Nova1/2 dKO embryos.
source: In addition, quantitative and semi-quantitative RT-PCR showed that most alternative sequences in the promoter and coding regions were not affected; however, the inclusion of microexon 6b in both Robo1 and Robo2 was significantly increased in Nova1/2 dKO embryos (Figure 3A,B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR shown in Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The inclusion of exon 6b was sensitive to Nova1/2 gene copy number.
source: The inclusion of exon 6b was sensitive to Nova1/2 gene copy number (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), which is consistent with the dose-sensitive interaction between NOVAs and their targets (Darnell, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and a citation to a previous publication (Darnell, 2006).

claim: Both Nova1 Het; Nova2 KO and Nova1/2 dKO embryos had midline crossing failure, with the defect being more severe in Nova1/2 dKO animals.
source: Similar to the DCC-related guidance defect (Leggere et al., 2016), both Nova1 Het; Nova2 KO and Nova1/2 dKO embryos had midline crossing failure, with the defect being more severe in Nova1/2 dKO animals, whereas the other genotype combinations, including Nova1/2 dHet mutants, were phenotypically normal.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and a citation to a previous publication (Leggere et al., 2016).

claim: Exon 6b encodes a short linker between the extracellular third and fourth Ig domains, which is conserved in mammals and chickens.
source: Exon 6b encodes a short linker between the extracellular third and fourth Ig domains, which is conserved in mammals and chickens (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The inclusion of the alternative exon 21 in Robo2 was somewhat reduced in Nova1/2 dKO embryos.
source: The inclusion of the alternative exon 21 in Robo2, which encodes an intracellular region between the CC1 and CC2 domains, was somewhat reduced in Nova1/2 dKO embryos (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Nova1 or Nova2 overexpression reduced e6b+ levels in splicing reporter assays.
source: When Nova1 or Nova2 was overexpressed, e6b+ was reduced, consistent with the observation that e6b+ was abnormally increased in Nova1/2 dKO mutants (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from splicing assays shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Mutating candidate NOVA-binding sites in either intron 6 or intron 6b attenuated NOVA-mediated repression of eb6+.
source: When candidate NOVA-binding sites in either intron 6 or intron 6b were mutated from YCAY (Y = C/U) to YAAY (Buckanovich and Darnell, 1997), NOVA-mediated repression of eb6+ was attenuated.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from splicing assays and a citation to a previous publication (Buckanovich and Darnell, 1997).

claim: Mutations in both introns almost completely blocked NOVAs from reducing e6b+.
source: Mutations in both introns almost completely blocked NOVAs from reducing e6b+ (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from splicing assays shown in Figure 3D.

claim: NOVAs bind to intron sequences flanking exon 6b and prevent its inclusion into the mRNA product.
source: Thus, NOVAs bind to intron sequences flanking exon 6b and prevent its inclusion into the mRNA product.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the splicing assay results.

claim: Nova1 or Nova2 overexpression did not alter the exon 21 splicing pattern in Robo2.
source: We found that Nova1 or Nova2 overexpression did not alter the exon 21 splicing pattern, and that mutating candidate NOVA-binding sites in intron 20 also had no effect (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from splicing assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: NOVAs by themselves do not appear to directly control exon 21 alternative splicing.
source: Thus, NOVAs by themselves do not appear to directly control exon 21 alternative splicing.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the splicing assay results.

claim: NOVAs may cooperate with or function indirectly through other splicing factors to exert their effect on exon 21.
source: They may cooperate with or function indirectly through other splicing factors to exert their effect on exon 21.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the observation that NOVAs do not directly control exon 21 splicing.

claim: Deleting one copy of exon 6b from Robo1/2 genomic DNA in Nova1/2 dKO embryos restored e6b+ expression to a comparable level as in the WT.
source: In the Nova1/2 dKO background, the WT allele predominantly expressed e6b+ (Figure 3A; Figure 4A), whereas the deletion allele only produced e6b- (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D). The combination between the WT and deletion alleles generated the two isoforms at a similar ratio to that in the WT at E11.5 (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Deleting exon 6b in Robo1 and/or Robo2 did not alter the total mRNA or protein levels.
source: Deleting exon 6b in Robo1 and/or Robo2 did not alter the total mRNA or protein levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C), and did not affect the splicing of the surrounding areas or of other alternative exons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Deleting exon 6b in Robo1 and/or Robo2 did not affect the splicing of the surrounding areas or of other alternative exons.
source: Deleting exon 6b in Robo1 and/or Robo2 did not alter the total mRNA or protein levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C), and did not affect the splicing of the surrounding areas or of other alternative exons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Reducing Robo1(e6b+) alone partially restored midline crossing in Nova1/2 dKO mutants.
source: Using DiI labeling, we found that reducing Robo1(e6b+) alone partially restored midline crossing in Nova1/2 dKO mutants, whereas reducing Robo2(e6b+) alone had no effect (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DiI labeling shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Reducing Robo2(e6b+) alone had no effect on midline crossing in Nova1/2 dKO mutants.
source: Using DiI labeling, we found that reducing Robo1(e6b+) alone partially restored midline crossing in Nova1/2 dKO mutants, whereas reducing Robo2(e6b+) alone had no effect (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DiI labeling shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Reducing both Robo1(e6b+) and Robo2(e6b+) together further rescued the midline crossing defect in Nova1/2 dKO mutants.
source: Reducing both Robo1(e6b+) and Robo2(e6b+) together further rescued the midline crossing defect (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DiI labeling shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: SLIT/ROBO signaling has been shown to direct the lateral positioning of longitudinal axons.
source: After crossing the midline, commissural axons join longitudinal tracts that traverse parallel to the floorplate at different dorso-ventral positions. SLIT/ROBO signaling has been shown to direct the lateral positioning of longitudinal axons (Farmer et al., 2008; Jaworski et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2011; Long et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Farmer et al., 2008; Jaworski et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2011; Long et al., 2004).

claim: The ventral tract close to the midline was reduced in Nova1/2 dKO spinal cords.
source: We found that the ventral tract close to the midline was reduced, whereas the lateral tract was enlarged in Nova1/2 dKO spinal cords (Figure 4B,C), suggesting that some longitudinal axons projected further away from the midline.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from anti-L1 staining shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: The lateral tract was enlarged in Nova1/2 dKO spinal cords.
source: We found that the ventral tract close to the midline was reduced, whereas the lateral tract was enlarged in Nova1/2 dKO spinal cords (Figure 4B,C), suggesting that some longitudinal axons projected further away from the midline.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from anti-L1 staining shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Some longitudinal axons projected further away from the midline in Nova1/2 dKO spinal cords.
source: We found that the ventral tract close to the midline was reduced, whereas the lateral tract was enlarged in Nova1/2 dKO spinal cords (Figure 4B,C), suggesting that some longitudinal axons projected further away from the midline.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed changes in ventral and lateral tract sizes.

claim: Reducing Robo1(e6b+) alone in Nova1/2 dKO embryos partially reversed the lateral positioning defect.
source: We also found that reducing Robo1(e6b+) alone in Nova1/2 dKO embryos partially reversed this defect, whereas reducing Robo2(e6b+) alone had no effect (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from anti-L1 staining shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Reducing Robo2(e6b+) alone had no effect on the lateral positioning defect in Nova1/2 dKO embryos.
source: We also found that reducing Robo1(e6b+) alone in Nova1/2 dKO embryos partially reversed this defect, whereas reducing Robo2(e6b+) alone had no effect (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from anti-L1 staining shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Reducing both Robo1(e6b+) and Robo2(e6b+) largely rescued the lateral positioning defect in Nova1/2 dKO embryos.
source: Reducing both Robo1(e6b+) and Robo2(e6b+) largely rescued the defect (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from anti-L1 staining shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: The overall patterns of ROBO1/2 expression were comparable between WT and Nova1/2 dKO embryos.
source: The overall patterns of ROBO1/2 expression, which are low on precrossing axons and are highly upregulated on postcrossing axons, were comparable between WT and Nova1/2 dKO embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,C.

claim: Netrin/DCC signaling has been shown to control postcrossing commissural axon trajectories in the hindbrain, but not in the spinal cord.
source: Netrin/DCC signaling has been shown to control postcrossing commissural axon trajectories in the hindbrain, but not in the spinal cord.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: In Netrin1 or Dcc KO mutants, hindbrain commissural axons project at larger angles away from the midline.
source: In Netrin1 or Dcc KO mutants, hindbrain commissural axons project at larger angles away from the midline, whereas spinal commissural axons have normal postcrossing projection (Shoja-Taheri et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication (Shoja-Taheri et al., 2015).

claim: Spinal commissural axons have normal postcrossing projection in Netrin1 or Dcc KO mutants.
source: In Netrin1 or Dcc KO mutants, hindbrain commissural axons project at larger angles away from the midline, whereas spinal commissural axons have normal postcrossing projection (Shoja-Taheri et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication (Shoja-Taheri et al., 2015).

claim: Dcc KO mutants had a slight increase in the lateral funiculi.
source: Dcc KO mutants had a slight increase in the lateral funiculi, which was much less severe than in Nova1/2 dKO embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from anti-L1 staining shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: In Dcc KO embryos, some lateral axons evaded the medial spinal cord.
source: In Dcc KO embryos, some lateral axons evaded the medial spinal cord, which could result from axon defasiculation and/or from a lack of restrictive signal from the medial spinal cord.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations and inference.

claim: Defasiculation is observed in precrossing axons in Dcc KO, but not in Nova1/2 dKO embryos.
source: Defasiculation is observed in precrossing axons in Dcc KO, but not in Nova1/2 dKO embryos (Leggere et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2014), possibly due to the fact that DCCshort is still present in Nova1/2 dKO mutants, which may be sufficient for axonal adhesion.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Leggere et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2014).

claim: DCCshort is still present in Nova1/2 dKO mutants, which may be sufficient for axonal adhesion.
source: Defasiculation is observed in precrossing axons in Dcc KO, but not in Nova1/2 dKO embryos (Leggere et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2014), possibly due to the fact that DCCshort is still present in Nova1/2 dKO mutants, which may be sufficient for axonal adhesion.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the observation that defasciculation is not observed in Nova1/2 dKO embryos.

claim: In Dcc; Nova1; Nova2 triple KO embryos, the lateral funiculi were enlarged and most lateral axons projected into the medial spinal cord.
source: In Dcc; Nova1; Nova2 triple KO embryos, the lateral funiculi were enlarged and most lateral axons projected into the medial spinal cord.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: The defects in the Dcc; Nova1; Nova2 triple KO mutants appear to be a combination of those seen in Dcc and Nova1/2 KO mutants.
source: Thus, the defects in the triple KO mutants appear to be a combination of those seen in Dcc and Nova1/2 KO mutants.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed phenotypes.

claim: The lateral positioning defect in Nova1/2 dKO embryos cannot result solely from a deficiency in DCC signaling.
source: Taken together, the lateral positioning defect in Nova1/2 dKO embryos cannot result solely from a deficiency in DCC signaling, although loss of Dcc may contribute to a small degree.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the comparison of phenotypes in different mutants.

claim: Loss of Dcc may contribute to a small degree to the lateral positioning defect in Nova1/2 dKO embryos.
source: Taken together, the lateral positioning defect in Nova1/2 dKO embryos cannot result solely from a deficiency in DCC signaling, although loss of Dcc may contribute to a small degree.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the comparison of phenotypes in different mutants.

claim: Robo1(e6b-) expression partially blocked midline crossing, with ~30% of the axons failing to cross in chicken embryos.
source: We found that Robo1(e6b-) expression partially blocked midline crossing, with ~30% of the axons failing to cross.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in ovo electroporation in chicken embryos.

claim: Robo1(e6b+) further blocked midline crossing, with ~49% of the axons being unable to cross in chicken embryos.
source: Robo1(e6b+) further blocked midline crossing, with ~49% of the axons being unable to cross (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in ovo electroporation in chicken embryos shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: e6b+ appears to have a stronger repulsive effect than e6b-.
source: Thus, e6b+ appears to have a stronger repulsive effect than e6b-.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the comparison of midline crossing defects.

claim: Robo1(e6b+) overexpression blocked about half of the axons from crossing the midline in Robo3 Het embryos.
source: Robo1(e6b+) overexpression blocked about half of the axons from crossing the midline, whereas Robo1(e6b-) overexpression caused a milder defect (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), consistent with their effects in chickens.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole embryo culture shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Robo1(e6b-) overexpression caused a milder midline crossing defect than Robo1(e6b+) in Robo3 Het embryos.
source: Robo1(e6b+) overexpression blocked about half of the axons from crossing the midline, whereas Robo1(e6b-) overexpression caused a milder defect (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), consistent with their effects in chickens.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole embryo culture shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Robo1(e6b-) ectopic expression in chicken embryos directed commissural axons to travel closely to the midline within the ventral funiculi.
source: In addition, Robo1(e6b-) ectopic expression in chicken embryos directed commissural axons that had reached the contralateral side or abnormally stayed on the ipsilateral side to travel closely to the midline within the ventral funiculi (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in ovo electroporation shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Robo1(e6b+) ectopic expression guided axons further away from the midline to a more dorsolateral position than normal in chicken embryos.
source: In contrast, Robo1(e6b+) ectopic expression guided axons further away from the midline to a more dorsolateral position than normal (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in ovo electroporation shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Robo1(e6b-) and Robo1(e6b+) have distinct activities in guiding postcrossing commissural axons.
source: Thus, Robo1(e6b-) and Robo1(e6b+) have distinct activities in guiding postcrossing commissural axons.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed differences in axon guidance.

claim: Robo1 e6bΔ/Δ embryos had enlarged ventral funiculi.
source: Using anti-L1 staining, we also examined the positioning of longitudinal axons in homozygous exon 6b deletion mice, and found that Robo1 e6bΔ/Δ embryos, which produced exclusively e6b- (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), had enlarged ventral funiculi (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), consistent with the observation that e6b- directed axons close to the midline in chickens (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from anti-L1 staining shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Ectopic expression of Robo2(e6b-; e21-) did not affect midline crossing in chicken embryos.
source: We found that ectopic expression of Robo2(e6b-; e21-) did not affect midline crossing (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in ovo electroporation shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Expression of Robo2(e6b+; e21-), Robo2(e6b-; e21+), or Robo2(e6b+; e21+) similarly blocked about half of the axons from crossing in chicken embryos.
source: In contrast, expression of Robo2(e6b+; e21-), Robo2(e6b-; e21+), or Robo2(e6b+; e21+) similarly blocked about half of the axons from crossing (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in ovo electroporation shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: The inclusion of four amino acids in the extracellular domain from exon 6b increases ROBO2 repulsion.
source: Thus, the inclusion of four amino acids in the extracellular domain from exon 6b or the inclusion of 42 amino acids in the intracellular domain from exon 21 similarly increases ROBO2 repulsion.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the comparison of ROBO2 isoform activities.

claim: The inclusion of 42 amino acids in the intracellular domain from exon 21 increases ROBO2 repulsion.
source: Thus, the inclusion of four amino acids in the extracellular domain from exon 6b or the inclusion of 42 amino acids in the intracellular domain from exon 21 similarly increases ROBO2 repulsion.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the comparison of ROBO2 isoform activities.

claim: The effects of exon 6b and exon 21 inclusions on ROBO2 repulsion are neither synergistic nor additive.
source: The effects of these exon inclusions are neither synergistic nor additive.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the comparison of ROBO2 isoform activities.

claim: In the absence of the exon 21 coding sequence, e6b+ appears to be more repulsive than e6b- in ROBO2.
source: Taken together, in the absence of the exon 21 coding sequence, e6b+ appears to be more repulsive than e6b-.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the comparison of ROBO2 isoform activities.

claim: In the presence of exon 21, e6b- and e6b+ are comparable in their activities in ROBO2.
source: In the presence of exon 21, e6b- and e6b+ are comparable in their activities.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the comparison of ROBO2 isoform activities.

claim: Ectopic expression of all Robo2 isoforms directed postcrossing axons to comparable lateral positions as in GFP-expressing controls in chicken embryos.
source: Ectopic expression of all Robo2 isoforms directed postcrossing axons to comparable lateral positions as in GFP-expressing controls (Figure 5A,B), indicating similar activities among ROBO2 variants in guiding longitudinal axons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in ovo electroporation shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: ROBO2 variants have similar activities in guiding longitudinal axons.
source: Ectopic expression of all Robo2 isoforms directed postcrossing axons to comparable lateral positions as in GFP-expressing controls (Figure 5A,B), indicating similar activities among ROBO2 variants in guiding longitudinal axons.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed similar lateral positioning.

claim: Robo2 e6bΔ/Δ homozygous mutants had normal dorso-ventral positioning of longitudinal tracts.
source: Consistent with these findings, Robo2 e6bΔ/Δ homozygous mutants had normal dorso-ventral positioning of longitudinal tracts (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from anti-L1 staining shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The electroporated Robo1/2 isoforms were expressed at comparable levels in chicken embryos.
source: Using immunohistochemistry and western blotting, we found that the electroporated Robo1/2 isoforms were expressed at comparable levels in chicken embryos and that the exogenously expressed receptors could be detected on both pre- and post-crossing axons (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemistry and western blotting shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: The exogenously expressed ROBO1/2 receptors could be detected on both pre- and post-crossing axons in chicken embryos.
source: Using immunohistochemistry and western blotting, we found that the electroporated Robo1/2 isoforms were expressed at comparable levels in chicken embryos and that the exogenously expressed receptors could be detected on both pre- and post-crossing axons (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: The ROBO1 or ROBO2 isoforms were inserted into the surface of COS-1 cells at comparable levels.
source: Using cell surface biotinylation assays, we found that the ROBO1 or ROBO2 isoforms were inserted into the surface of COS-1 cells at comparable levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from cell surface biotinylation assays shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The ROBO1 or ROBO2 isoforms had comparable binding affinities toward SLIT2 (N-term).
source: We then compared the binding between the ROBO variants with an AP-SLIT2 (N-term) fusion protein in COS-1 cells. We found that the ROBO1 or ROBO2 isoforms had comparable binding affinities toward SLIT2 (N-term) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), consistent with the fact that the isoforms share the same SLIT-binding domain (Figure 3A) (Morlot et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from binding assays shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and a citation to a previous publication (Morlot et al., 2007).

claim: The ROBO1/2 isoforms share the same SLIT-binding domain.
source: We found that the ROBO1 or ROBO2 isoforms had comparable binding affinities toward SLIT2 (N-term) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), consistent with the fact that the isoforms share the same SLIT-binding domain (Figure 3A) (Morlot et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication (Morlot et al., 2007).

claim: Activation of the SLIT/ROBO pathway inhibits CDC42.
source: The RHO family of small GTPases have been shown to mediate SLIT/ROBO signaling during cell migration and axon guidance (Bashaw and Klein, 2010). Activation of the SLIT/ROBO pathway inhibits CDC42, activates RAC1, and has distinct effects on RHOA in different cell types (Fan et al., 2003; Guan et al., 2007; Wong et al., 2001; Yang and Bashaw, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Bashaw and Klein, 2010; Fan et al., 2003; Guan et al., 2007; Wong et al., 2001; Yang and Bashaw, 2006).

claim: Activation of the SLIT/ROBO pathway activates RAC1.
source: The RHO family of small GTPases have been shown to mediate SLIT/ROBO signaling during cell migration and axon guidance (Bashaw and Klein, 2010). Activation of the SLIT/ROBO pathway inhibits CDC42, activates RAC1, and has distinct effects on RHOA in different cell types (Fan et al., 2003; Guan et al., 2007; Wong et al., 2001; Yang and Bashaw, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Bashaw and Klein, 2010; Fan et al., 2003; Guan et al., 2007; Wong et al., 2001; Yang and Bashaw, 2006).

claim: Activation of the SLIT/ROBO pathway has distinct effects on RHOA in different cell types.
source: The RHO family of small GTPases have been shown to mediate SLIT/ROBO signaling during cell migration and axon guidance (Bashaw and Klein, 2010). Activation of the SLIT/ROBO pathway inhibits CDC42, activates RAC1, and has distinct effects on RHOA in different cell types (Fan et al., 2003; Guan et al., 2007; Wong et al., 2001; Yang and Bashaw, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Fan et al., 2003; Guan et al., 2007; Wong et al., 2001; Yang and Bashaw, 2006).

claim: Both ROBO1 isoforms inhibited CDC42 and activated RAC1, with e6b+ exerting a stronger effect than e6b-.
source: We found that both ROBO1 isoforms inhibited CDC42 and activated RAC1, with e6b+ exerting a stronger effect than e6b- (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from small GTPase activation assays shown in Figure 6.

claim: Among the four ROBO2 isoforms, e6b-; e21- had no effect on either CDC42 or RAC1.
source: Among the four ROBO2 isoforms, e6b-; e21- had no effect on either CDC42 or RAC1, while the other three similarly inhibited CDC42 and activated RAC1 (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from small GTPase activation assays shown in Figure 6.

claim: Three ROBO2 isoforms (e6b+; e21-, e6b-; e21+, e6b+; e21+) similarly inhibited CDC42 and activated RAC1.
source: Among the four ROBO2 isoforms, e6b-; e21- had no effect on either CDC42 or RAC1, while the other three similarly inhibited CDC42 and activated RAC1 (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from small GTPase activation assays shown in Figure 6.

claim: No significant changes in RHOA activation were observed in COS-1 cells expressing any of the ROBO isoforms upon SLIT2 N-term stimulation.
source: We did not observe significant changes in RHOA activation in the COS-1 cells expressing any of the isoforms upon SLIT2 N-term stimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations from small GTPase activation assays.

claim: Robo2(e6b-;e21-), the only isoform that does not block midline crossing when ectopically expressed, has no effect on CDC42/RAC1.
source: Taken together, Robo2(e6b-;e21-), the only isoform that does not block midline crossing when ectopically expressed (Figure 5), has no effect on CDC42/RAC1 (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the comparison of functional and signaling data.

claim: Other ROBO1/2 isoforms inhibit CDC42 and activate RAC1 following SLIT2 binding.
source: By contrast, other ROBO1/2 isoforms inhibit CDC42 and activate RAC1 following SLIT2 binding.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the small GTPase activation assay results.

claim: Between the ROBO1 isoforms, e6b+ has a stronger effect on CDC42/RAC1 than e6b-.
source: Between the ROBO1 isoforms, e6b+ has a stronger effect than e6b-.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the small GTPase activation assay results.

claim: Robo1/2(e6b+) was the predominant form at E11 in rat dorsal spinal cord.
source: We found that Robo1/2(e6b+) was the predominant form at E11, and that over time, Robo1/2(e6b+) decreased while Robo1/2(e6b-) increased (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Over time from E11 to E14, Robo1/2(e6b+) decreased while Robo1/2(e6b-) increased in rat dorsal spinal cord.
source: We found that Robo1/2(e6b+) was the predominant form at E11, and that over time, Robo1/2(e6b+) decreased while Robo1/2(e6b-) increased (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The switch in the e6b isoform levels coincided with a steady increase in Nova1/2 expression over E11 to E14.
source: The switch in the e6b isoform levels coincided with a steady increase in Nova1/2 expression over this period (Figure 7B), which represses e6b+ production (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR shown in Figure 7B.

claim: NOVAs repress e6b+ production.
source: The switch in the e6b isoform levels coincided with a steady increase in Nova1/2 expression over this period (Figure 7B), which represses e6b+ production (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from splicing assays shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The ventral commissure in Robo1 e6bΔ/Δ mutants was thicker than in the WT controls at the lumbar level at E10.5.
source: The ventral commissures in Robo1 e6bΔ/Δ and Robo1/2 e6bΔ/Δ mutants were thicker than in the WT controls at the lumbar level.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from anti-ROBO3 staining.

claim: The ventral commissure in Robo1/2 e6bΔ/Δ mutants was thicker than in the WT controls at the lumbar level at E10.5.
source: The ventral commissures in Robo1 e6bΔ/Δ and Robo1/2 e6bΔ/Δ mutants were thicker than in the WT controls at the lumbar level.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from anti-ROBO3 staining.

claim: All genotypes had comparable ventral commissure thickness at the brachial level at E10.5.
source: All genotypes had comparable ventral commissure thickness at the brachial level.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from anti-ROBO3 staining.

claim: A larger number of axons had reached and crossed the midline in Robo1 e6bΔ/Δ mutants than in the WT controls at E10.5 lumbar level.
source: This suggests that a larger number of axons had reached and crossed the midline in the mutants than in the WT controls.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed thicker ventral commissure.

claim: Robo2 e6bΔ/Δ mutants were indistinguishable from the WT at E10.5 lumbar level.
source: We also found that Robo2 e6bΔ/Δ mutants were indistinguishable from the WT, whereas Robo1/2 e6bΔ/Δ double mutants displayed a similar phenotype to that in Robo1 e6bΔ/Δ single mutants (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from anti-ROBO3 staining shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: Robo1/2 e6bΔ/Δ double mutants displayed a similar phenotype to that in Robo1 e6bΔ/Δ single mutants at E10.5 lumbar level.
source: We also found that Robo2 e6bΔ/Δ mutants were indistinguishable from the WT, whereas Robo1/2 e6bΔ/Δ double mutants displayed a similar phenotype to that in Robo1 e6bΔ/Δ single mutants (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from anti-ROBO3 staining shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: Robo1(e6b+), but not Robo2(e6b+), appears to prevent premature midline crossing by commissural axons.
source: Thus, Robo1(e6b+), but not Robo2(e6b+), appears to prevent premature midline crossing by commissural axons.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the comparison of phenotypes in different mutants.

claim: The lack of Robo1(e6b+) allows commissural axons to cross the midline earlier, but does not permit additional axons to cross.
source: Thus, the lack of Robo1(e6b+) allows commissural axons to cross the midline earlier, but does not permit additional axons to cross.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that mutants become indistinguishable from WT at later stages.

claim: ROBO-mediated repulsion has traditionally been thought to be repressed before crossing, and then to become upregulated after crossing.
source: As commissural axons navigate across the CNS midline, ROBO-mediated repulsion has traditionally been thought to be repressed before crossing, and then to become upregulated after crossing.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Mammalian ROBO1 and ROBO2 are not uniformly inhibited precrossing and are instead subject to additional temporal control via alternative splicing at a conserved microexon.
source: Here, we report that mammalian ROBO1 and ROBO2 are not uniformly inhibited precrossing and are instead subject to additional temporal control via alternative splicing at a conserved microexon.
evidence: The claim is a primary finding of the study supported by multiple experimental data.

claim: The NOVA splicing factors regulate the developmental expression of ROBO1 and ROBO2 variants with small sequence differences and distinct guidance activities.
source: The NOVA splicing factors regulate the developmental expression of ROBO1 and ROBO2 variants with small sequence differences and distinct guidance activities.
evidence: The claim is a primary finding of the study supported by multiple experimental data.

claim: ROBO-mediated axonal repulsion is activated early in development to prevent premature crossing.
source: As a result, ROBO-mediated axonal repulsion is activated early in development to prevent premature crossing and becomes inhibited later to allow crossing.
evidence: The claim is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from exon 6b deletion mutants.

claim: ROBO-mediated axonal repulsion becomes inhibited later to allow crossing.
source: As a result, ROBO-mediated axonal repulsion is activated early in development to prevent premature crossing and becomes inhibited later to allow crossing.
evidence: The claim is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from Nova1/2 dKO and rescue experiments.

claim: Postcrossing, the ROBO1 and ROBO2 isoforms are disinhibited to prevent midline reentry and to guide postcrossing commissural axons to distinct mediolateral positions.
source: Postcrossing, the ROBO1 and ROBO2 isoforms are disinhibited to prevent midline reentry and to guide postcrossing commissural axons to distinct mediolateral positions.
evidence: The claim is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from ectopic expression and mutant analyses.

claim: Within the spinal commissural axons, Netrin/DCC signaling is activated to promote midline attraction while SLIT/ROBO signaling that mediates repulsion is inhibited prior to crossing.
source: Within the spinal commissural axons, Netrin/DCC (Deleted in colorectal carcinoma) signaling is activated to promote midline attraction while SLIT/ROBO (Roundabout) signaling that mediates repulsion is inhibited prior to crossing.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Following crossing, SLIT/ROBO signaling becomes upregulated to facilitate midline expulsion and to block midline reentry.
source: Following crossing, SLIT/ROBO signaling becomes upregulated to facilitate midline expulsion and to block midline reentry (Evans and Bashaw, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication (Evans and Bashaw, 2010).

claim: SLIT/ROBO signaling is evolutionarily conserved and plays an important role in various biological processes, including cell migration, axon guidance, angiogenesis, and organogenesis.
source: SLIT/ROBO signaling is evolutionarily conserved and plays an important role in various biological processes, including cell migration, axon guidance, angiogenesis, and organogenesis (Blockus and Chédotal, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication (Blockus and Chédotal, 2016).

claim: In Drosophila, Comm blocks ROBO insertion into the axonal surface.
source: In Drosophila, Comm blocks ROBO insertion into the axonal surface (Keleman et al., 2002; Keleman et al., 2005).

claim: In vertebrates, PRRG4 represses ROBO1 surface trafficking.
source: In vertebrates, PRRG4 (Proline-rich and Gla domain 4) represses ROBO1 surface trafficking, whereas USP33 (Ubiquitin-specific peptidase 33), RabGDI/GDI1 (GDP dissociation inhibitor 1), and CLSTN1 (Calsyntenin1) stabilize or promote ROBO1 surface localization (Alther et al., 2016; Justice et al., 2017; Philipp et al., 2012; Yuasa-Kawada et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Alther et al., 2016; Justice et al., 2017; Philipp et al., 2012; Yuasa-Kawada et al., 2009).

claim: USP33, RabGDI/GDI1, and CLSTN1 stabilize or promote ROBO1 surface localization.
source: In vertebrates, PRRG4 (Proline-rich and Gla domain 4) represses ROBO1 surface trafficking, whereas USP33 (Ubiquitin-specific peptidase 33), RabGDI/GDI1 (GDP dissociation inhibitor 1), and CLSTN1 (Calsyntenin1) stabilize or promote ROBO1 surface localization (Alther et al., 2016; Justice et al., 2017; Philipp et al., 2012; Yuasa-Kawada et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Alther et al., 2016; Justice et al., 2017; Philipp et al., 2012; Yuasa-Kawada et al., 2009).

source: In addition, miR-92 has been shown to suppress vertebrate ROBO1 protein translation (Yang et al., 2018).

source: The mammalian Robo genes undergo alternative splicing to produce variants with complex expression patterns and guidance activities (Chen et al., 2008; Clark et al., 2002; Dalkic et al., 2006; Yuan et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Chen et al., 2008; Clark et al., 2002; Dalkic et al., 2006; Yuan et al., 1999).

source: Robo1 and Robo2 share a homologous alternative exon 6b, which is 9 and 12 bp in length, respectively.

claim: Alternatively spliced 'microexons' (≤51 bp) are highly conserved in the nervous system.
source: Recent studies demonstrate that alternatively spliced 'microexons' (≤51 bp) are highly conserved in the nervous system and are frequently misregulated in autistic individuals (Irimia et al., 2014; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Irimia et al., 2014; Li et al., 2015).

claim: Microexons are frequently misregulated in autistic individuals.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Irimia et al., 2014; Li et al., 2015).

claim: The alternative splicing of Robo1/2 at microexon 6b is crucial for axon guidance and is controlled by the NOVA family of splicing factors.
source: Here, we report that the alternative splicing of Robo1 and Robo2 (referred to herein as Robo1/2) at microexon 6b is crucial for axon guidance and is controlled by the NOVA (Neuro-oncological ventral antigen) family of splicing factors, which are neural-specific KH (hnRNP K homology)-type RNA-binding proteins (Darnell, 2006).
evidence: The claim is a primary finding of the study supported by multiple experimental data and a citation to a previous publication (Darnell, 2006).

claim: Loss of Nova1 and Nova2 alters the expression of exon 6b and leads to severe midline crossing and postcrossing guidance defects.
source: We show that loss of Nova1 and Nova2 (referred to herein as Nova1/2) alters the expression of exon 6b and leads to severe midline crossing and postcrossing guidance defects.
evidence: The claim is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Genetically restoring the normal expression profiles of Robo1/2 exon 6b is able to reverse the defects in Nova1/2 mutants.
source: Genetically restoring the normal expression profiles of Robo1/2 exon 6b is able to reverse these defects in Nova1/2 mutants.
evidence: The claim is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from genetic rescue experiments.

claim: Exon 6b alternative isoforms display distinct guidance activities and their production is developmentally regulated.
source: Interestingly, exon 6b alternative isoforms display distinct guidance activities and their production is developmentally regulated.
evidence: The claim is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from ectopic expression and developmental expression analyses.

claim: ROBO repulsion is not uniformly repressed precrossing as previously believed, but is instead activated initially to block premature crossing and is sufficiently blocked during crossing.
source: Consequently, ROBO-mediated repulsion is not uniformly repressed precrossing as previously believed, but is instead activated initially to block premature crossing and is sufficiently blocked during crossing.
evidence: The claim is a primary finding of the study based on inference from multiple experimental data.

claim: Mammalian ROBO1/2 are subject to complex regulation, which is coordinated by alternative splicing, protein translation and trafficking, and activity inhibition by Robo3.
source: Together, our study demonstrates that mammalian ROBO1/2 are subject to complex regulation, which is coordinated by alternative splicing, protein translation and trafficking, and activity inhibition by Robo3.
evidence: The claim is a primary conclusion of the study based on inference from multiple experimental data.
